title: The Toughest Animal Alive
principle: Stopping completely and starting again later is called cryptobiosis.

t: There is an animal in your gutter that survives being frozen solid, boiled, and thrown into space.
Tardigrades tolerate temperatures near absolute zero, hard vacuum, and radiation doses thousands of times lethal for a human. They are also about half a millimetre long and live in moss.
sub: And the way it does it is stranger than the list.
The trick is not toughness. That is the part worth getting right.

question: A tardigrade survives boiling and freezing and space. What is it doing while all that happens?
What is the physiological state during extreme tolerance?
options: Nothing at all — it has stopped completely
Running on a different kind of energy
stages.outcome: Nothing at all — it has stopped completely
note: Commit. Ask what a cell would have to keep doing to stay alive, and whether any of it is possible at −272 °C.

stages.label: How bad does it get?
captions: Active in a film of water: it needs oxygen, food, and roughly the temperatures you do.
The water dries up. Over a few hours it pulls in its legs and shrinks into a barrel called a tun.
As a tun it survives years without water. Add a drop and it walks away.
Cooled to one degree above absolute zero, and it still revives.
Ten days in open space: the vacuum did not kill them. Full solar ultraviolet, on top of the vacuum, mostly did.
t: Push the conditions from ordinary to impossible and watch what the animal does about it.
The tolerance envelope, in the order it was established. Note where the last caption stops being a success.
after: It does not fight any of it. It switches itself off first.
The active animal is unremarkable — it drowns, starves and overheats like anything else its size. Everything on this slider is a property of the tun, and the tun is not a running organism.

t: Stopping completely and starting again later is called cryptobiosis. Hidden life.
Cryptobiosis is a reversible suspension of metabolism. Measured activity falls below a ten-thousandth of normal, which is to say below anything that can be detected at all.
Losing water is the trigger. As the animal dries, specialised disordered proteins turn the cytoplasm into a glass, immobilising everything inside it so that nothing can react, drift or unfold.

That glass is the whole mechanism, and it explains the shape of the results. A vitrified organism has no chemistry to disrupt, so temperature and pressure have little to act on — but ionising radiation and ultraviolet damage molecules directly, without needing metabolism, and those are exactly the exposures that kill tuns. Tardigrades also carry a protein that binds DNA and shields it, which reduces radiation damage but does not abolish it.
sub: It is not asleep. Asleep is still doing things.
There is no heartbeat to slow down and no breathing to stop; the animal is chemically inert.
Which is why the question 'is a tun alive?' has no clean answer, and is a better question than it first appears.

It does not widen what life needs in order to run. A tardigrade in a moss cushion needs water, oxygen and food, exactly like anything else. What it can do is leave the running state and return, and that is a different claim — a much stranger one, and one with far more practical use.

q: What does a tardigrade surviving space actually prove?
What does cryptobiosis establish about the requirements of life?
Why does the distinction between tolerance and suspension matter?
options: That life can be paused and restarted, not that it can run on nothing
That living things can survive anywhere
why: While it was in space it was not doing anything. It was a dried-out speck. The clever bit is that it started again afterwards.
Nothing metabolised under those conditions. The result bounds the conditions a suspended organism can be carried through, not the conditions under which metabolism is possible.

Because the two support completely different conclusions. Suspension says a state can be preserved and resumed, which is a claim about stability. Tolerance would say chemistry proceeds under those conditions, which nothing here demonstrates — and conflating them is how a real and useful finding gets reported as evidence that life needs almost nothing.

t: If you could dry a vaccine the way a tardigrade dries itself, it would not need a fridge.

The glass-forming proteins are being engineered into human cells and into stored biological material for exactly this reason. Vaccines that survive a warm supply chain would reach places refrigeration cannot, and the mechanism being copied was found in an animal living in moss.
